body:
What is phishing?

Phishing is a deceptive technique in which a fraudster pretends to represent a trustworthy person or organisation and attempts to obtain sensitive information or persuade a user to perform an unsafe action.

The impersonated organisation may be a bank, government department, payment provider, delivery company or popular online service.

For example, a message may falsely state that a bank account will be suspended unless the recipient immediately verifies personal details through a supplied link. The apparent urgency encourages the recipient to act without checking whether the message is genuine.

Social engineering: the broader concept

Social engineering refers to manipulating people into revealing information or taking actions that compromise security. Rather than depending entirely on a technical weakness, the attacker exploits human responses such as trust, fear, urgency, curiosity or the expectation of receiving a benefit.

Phishing is a form of social engineering. A deceptive phone call or a fraudulent request to install remote-access software can also involve social engineering.

Common forms of phishing

FormCommunication mediumBasic characteristic
Email phishingEmailFraudulent email impersonating a trusted source.
SmishingSMS or text messageFraudulent message asking the recipient to visit a link, call a number or share information.
VishingVoice callCaller impersonates an authority or service provider to obtain confidential information or payment.

Phishing attempts may also appear through social-media messages, messaging applications and fake websites. The medium does not change the central feature: the attacker uses deception to obtain information or influence behaviour.

How deception leads to harm

A common phishing attempt contains several recognisable elements.

  • Impersonation: The communication appears to come from a familiar institution or person.
  • Pressure: The recipient is told to act urgently to avoid a penalty or obtain a benefit.
  • Unsafe request: The message asks for credentials, a payment, installation of an application or interaction with an unverified link.
  • Possible harm: The recipient may lose money, disclose sensitive information or compromise an account or device.

Recognising suspicious communications

Warning signs include unexpected requests for passwords or one-time passwords, threats of immediate account closure, unusually attractive offers, pressure to avoid independent verification and links that do not match the claimed organisation.

However, a fraudulent message may contain correct spelling, familiar branding and personal details. A legitimate-looking appearance is not proof of authenticity.

A secure connection is not proof of a genuine organisation

HTTPS indicates that communication with a website is protected in transit when implemented correctly. It does not, by itself, prove that the website operator is trustworthy. A fraudulent website can also use HTTPS.

Basic protection against phishing

  • Do not disclose passwords, PINs or OTPs in response to unsolicited requests.
  • Verify unexpected requests through an independently obtained official phone number, application or website.
  • Avoid opening suspicious links and attachments.
  • Use strong, unique passwords and enable multi-factor authentication where available.
  • Report suspicious activity through the appropriate institutional or cybercrime channel.

Phishing prevention depends especially on verifying the claimed identity and purpose of a communication. A firewall or anti-malware application may provide additional protection, but neither can reliably determine the honesty of every person requesting information.

Prelims focus

  • Phishing uses deceptive communication to obtain information or induce an unsafe action.
  • Social engineering manipulates human behaviour.
  • Smishing refers to phishing through SMS or text messages.
  • Vishing refers to voice-based deception.
  • Phishing can occur without installing malware.
  • Trap: HTTPS alone does not establish that a website is genuine.

[Sources: NIST, Small Business Cybersecurity Glossary, entries Phishing, Spear Phishing and Multi-factor Authentication, updated 9 April 2025; CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2024-0050, Preventing Online Scams, section Phishing Scams and Best Practices and Recommendations, issued 24 October 2024; Reserve Bank of India, Consumer Awareness: Cyber Threats and Frauds, press release dated 28 January 2022, sections Vishing, Phishing and Safe Digital Banking Practices; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: An adult woman in an Indian home cautiously studies an unexpected smartphone message, pausing before responding.
pictures.caption: A suspicious message may imitate a trusted institution and demand immediate action.

pictures.alt: Phishing uses impersonation, urgency or fear, and an unsafe request; independent official verification before responding can interrupt the path to harm.
pictures.caption: Recognising deception before responding can interrupt a common fraud sequence.

title: Phishing and Social Engineering: How Fraudsters Deceive Users

body:
Cybercrime does not always require malware

Many cyber-enabled financial frauds succeed because a person is deceived into sharing information, approving a payment or trusting an impersonator. The fraud may occur even when the victim's device contains no malicious software.

Recognising the distinction between a fraudulent transaction and malware infection helps in selecting the appropriate protection.

Common forms of cyber-enabled fraud

FraudHow the deception worksBasic safeguard
Fake KYC requestSomeone impersonates a bank or service provider and threatens account suspension unless details are supplied.Verify through the bank's official application, website or branch.
UPI collect-request fraudA fraudulent payment request is presented as a step needed to receive money.Check the payment request, recipient and amount before approving anything.
Fake customer-care fraudA fraudulent support number or caller is presented as an official service.Use contact details obtained independently from the official provider.
Remote-support scamA caller claims that a device or account needs urgent repair and asks for remote access.Do not grant remote control to an unverified person.
Digital arrest scamFraudsters impersonate officials, threaten legal action and demand money to avoid supposed arrest or investigation.Do not transfer money under threats; independently contact legitimate authorities.
Fake job or investment offerFraudsters promise employment or unrealistic returns in exchange for advance payments or sensitive details.Verify the organisation and avoid payments made under pressure or unsupported promises.

Understanding UPI fraud

The Unified Payments Interface (UPI) enables digital payments between participating accounts and applications. Fraudsters sometimes misuse payment requests or deceive users about the purpose of a transaction.

A fundamental distinction is between receiving money and authorising a payment.

  • Receiving money: A person does not need to enter a UPI PIN or scan a QR code merely to receive an incoming payment.
  • Sending money: A UPI payment generally requires the payer to authorise the transaction using the applicable payment method, commonly a UPI PIN.
  • Collect request: A request to pay money may be legitimate or fraudulent. The payer must verify its purpose, recipient and amount before approving it.

Important UPI distinction

A request to enter a UPI PIN to receive a prize, refund or incoming transfer is a strong warning sign of fraud. Scanning a payee's QR code is ordinarily an action used to initiate a payment to that payee, not a requirement for receiving money.

OTP, PIN and account information

An OTP is a one-time password used in certain authentication or transaction-verification processes. A PIN is a personal identification number used to authenticate a user or authorise an action.

Fraudsters may request OTPs, PINs, passwords, card details or other confidential information while pretending to provide customer support, process refunds or update records.

A genuine banking transaction should be initiated and verified through trusted channels. A caller's claim to be a bank employee does not justify sharing confidential authentication information.

Identity theft and impersonation

Identity theft occurs when someone wrongfully obtains and uses another person's identifying information, typically for fraud or deception.

Impersonation occurs when someone falsely presents themselves as another person or institution. The 2 concepts may overlap, but they are not identical. A fraudster can impersonate a government officer during a call without necessarily stealing the officer's actual account credentials.

Safe behaviour during suspicious transactions

A user should verify the recipient's identity, examine payment details, avoid sharing confidential authentication information and refuse requests for remote access from unverified callers.

If money has been transferred fraudulently, the affected person should promptly contact the bank or payment provider and use the official cybercrime reporting mechanism. Quick reporting can support efforts to prevent further movement of funds, although recovery is not guaranteed.

Prelims focus

  • Vishing and fake customer-care calls are examples of social engineering.
  • A UPI PIN is not required merely to receive money.
  • A QR code supplied by a payee commonly supports initiation of a payment to that payee.
  • An OTP must not be disclosed to an unsolicited caller.
  • Digital arrest scams use false claims of official authority and threats of legal action.
  • Trap: Financial fraud does not necessarily imply that malware has infected the victim's device.

[Sources: Reserve Bank of India, Consumer Awareness: Cyber Threats and Frauds, press release dated 28 January 2022, sections Vishing, Remote Access, UPI Collect Request Fraud and Safe Digital Banking Practices; RBI, RBI Kehta Hai, Fraud Through UPI QR and Safeguards for Digital Banking; CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2024-0050, Preventing Online Scams, sections Tech Support Scams, Job Scams, Investment Scams and Digital Arrest, issued 24 October 2024; NIST, Small Business Cybersecurity Glossary, entry Identity Theft, updated 9 April 2025; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Incoming UPI money needs no PIN or QR scan; outgoing payments need authorisation, and collect requests ask you to pay.
pictures.caption: A UPI PIN is associated with payment authorisation, not merely receiving money.

title: Common Cyber Frauds: UPI Scams, Identity Theft and Impersonation

body:
Why different controls are needed

A computer or public information system faces several kinds of risk. Malicious software may operate on a device, an unauthorised connection may attempt to reach a network, and an outdated application may contain a known security weakness.

These risks are related, but they are not identical. Therefore, the protective measures used against them have different functions.

Firewall: controlling network communication

Firewall

A firewall is a hardware or software-based security control that monitors or restricts network communication according to established rules or policies.

A firewall can allow permitted connections and block connections that do not satisfy its rules. It may be used on an individual computer or at the boundary of an organisation's network.

For example, a public office may permit ordinary authorised communication with its online services while restricting unnecessary incoming connections to internal computers.

However, a firewall does not automatically prevent every cyber threat. It cannot be relied upon to stop a citizen from voluntarily disclosing an OTP to a fraudster, and it does not replace anti-malware software installed on a device.

Anti-malware software: identifying malicious programs

Anti-malware software is designed to detect, block and sometimes remove malicious programs. Antivirus software is a common form of anti-malware protection.

Security software may examine files, applications and device activity for indications of malware. It helps protect against several categories of harmful software, including viruses and spyware.

Its effectiveness depends on the threat, the detection capability and the state of the software. A new or previously unrecognised threat may escape detection.

Software updates and security patches

A software update is a newer version or modification of software. Updates may provide new features, correct errors or improve security.

A security patch is a correction intended to address a particular security weakness.

For example, if a software provider identifies a vulnerability that could allow unauthorised activity, the provider may release an update to correct it. Installing that update reduces exposure to the corrected weakness.

Updates should be obtained through trusted, official sources. An unexpected message instructing a user to install an alleged urgent security update may itself be fraudulent.

Comparing the 3 controls

ControlMain functionImportant limitation
FirewallControls network traffic according to rules.Does not prevent every malicious program or fraudulent request.
Anti-malwareDetects and blocks many malicious programs.Cannot guarantee detection of every threat.
Security updateCorrects known weaknesses in software.Does not prevent every type of fraud or misuse.

What about email filtering?

An organisation may also use email filtering to identify and restrict suspicious messages or attachments. This can reduce exposure to phishing and malicious files before they reach users.

Filtering is not infallible. Some harmful messages may still reach the inbox, so staff awareness and independent verification remain essential.

Choosing the appropriate control

If an office needs to restrict unnecessary incoming network connections, a firewall is directly relevant. If a device contains a malicious program, anti-malware protection is relevant. If an application contains a known weakness for which a security patch exists, installing the patch is relevant.

If a caller persuades an employee to disclose an OTP, none of these controls alone addresses the central problem as directly as verifying the caller and refusing to disclose authentication information.

Prelims focus

  • A firewall controls network communication according to security rules.
  • Anti-malware software helps detect and block malicious programs.
  • A security patch corrects a software weakness.
  • Automatic updates can help keep supported software current.
  • Email filtering reduces exposure to some malicious messages and attachments.
  • Trap: A firewall and antivirus software have different primary functions.

[Sources: NIST, Small Business Cybersecurity Glossary, entries Firewall, Antivirus/Anti-malware Software, Patch and Malware, updated 9 April 2025; NIST Computer Security Resource Center Glossary, entry Firewall, including definition from Special Publication 800-41 Revision 1; CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2025-0019, sections Patch Management, Secure Network and Endpoint Devices and Conduct Employee Awareness and Training, issued 10 May 2025; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A firewall controls network connections, anti-malware examines a device, and patches fix software weaknesses; fraudulent OTP requests need human verification.
pictures.caption: Different protective controls act at different points in the use of a digital system.

title: Firewalls, Anti-Malware Software and Updates: Understanding Their Functions
